claim: The role of cerebellum in controlling eye movements is well established.
source: The role of cerebellum in controlling eye movements is well established, but its contribution to more complex forms of visual behavior has remained elusive.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Inoshita and Hirano, 2018; Ivry and Diener, 1991; Kunimatsu et al., 2016) in the Introduction section.

claim: The cerebellum's contribution to more complex forms of visual behavior has remained elusive.
source: The role of cerebellum in controlling eye movements is well established, but its contribution to more complex forms of visual behavior has remained elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by the context of the study.

claim: Single-unit DN neurons modulated spiking activity over the entire time course of the task.
source: We found that single-unit DN neurons modulated spiking activity over the entire time course of the task, and that their activity often bridged temporally separated intra-trial events, yet in a heterogeneous manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: DN neuron activity often bridged temporally separated intra-trial events in a heterogeneous manner.
source: We found that single-unit DN neurons modulated spiking activity over the entire time course of the task, and that their activity often bridged temporally separated intra-trial events, yet in a heterogeneous manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the electrophysiological recordings and modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both NHPs showed different behavioral strategies which influenced performance.
source: Both NHPs showed different behavioral strategies, which influenced the performance.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral modeling and performance data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Activity of DN neurons reflected the unique strategies of the two NHPs.
source: Activity of the DN neurons reflected the unique strategies, with the direction of the visual stimulus frequently being encoded long before an upcoming saccade.
evidence: This is supported by the encoding model and decoding analysis presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The direction of the visual stimulus was frequently encoded long before an upcoming saccade.
source: Activity of the DN neurons reflected the unique strategies, with the direction of the visual stimulus frequently being encoded long before an upcoming saccade.
evidence: This is supported by the encoding model and temporal analysis of neural activity.

claim: The latency of ramping activity of DN neurons following presentation of the visual stimulus was shorter in the better performing NHP.
source: Moreover, the latency of the ramping activity of DN neurons following presentation of the visual stimulus was shorter in the better performing NHP.
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis and ramping onset detection presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: DN neurons predominantly receive inputs from Purkinje cells in the D1 and D2 zones of the lateral cerebellum.
source: Labeling with the retrograde tracer Cholera Toxin B in the recording location in the DN indicated that these neurons predominantly receive inputs from Purkinje cells in the D1 and D2 zones of the lateral cerebellum as well as neurons of the principal olive and medial pons, all regions known to connect with neurons in the prefrontal cortex contributing to planning of saccades.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data presented in Figure 5.

claim: DN neurons receive inputs from neurons of the principal olive and medial pons.
source: Labeling with the retrograde tracer Cholera Toxin B in the recording location in the DN indicated that these neurons predominantly receive inputs from Purkinje cells in the D1 and D2 zones of the lateral cerebellum as well as neurons of the principal olive and medial pons, all regions known to connect with neurons in the prefrontal cortex contributing to planning of saccades.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The principal olive and medial pons are regions known to connect with neurons in the prefrontal cortex contributing to planning of saccades.
source: Labeling with the retrograde tracer Cholera Toxin B in the recording location in the DN indicated that these neurons predominantly receive inputs from Purkinje cells in the D1 and D2 zones of the lateral cerebellum as well as neurons of the principal olive and medial pons, all regions known to connect with neurons in the prefrontal cortex contributing to planning of saccades.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: DN neurons can dynamically modulate their activity during a visual attention task comprising sensorimotor and cognitive attentional components.
source: Together, our results highlight that DN neurons can dynamically modulate their activity during a visual attention task, comprising not only sensorimotor but also cognitive attentional components.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: Evidence is emerging that the cerebellum participates in more complex cognitive visual functions.
source: Yet, over the last few decades evidence is emerging that the cerebellum also participates in more complex cognitive visual functions (Baier et al., 2010; Brissenden et al., 2016; Courchesne et al., 1994; Nicolson et al., 2001; Voogd et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The cerebellum uses visual information to guide the planning of saccades while interacting with areas such as the frontal eye fields, lateral intraparietal area, superior colliculus, and basal ganglia.
source: For example, while interacting with areas such as the frontal eye fields (FEFs), lateral intraparietal area, superior colliculus, and basal ganglia, the cerebellum uses visual information to guide the planning of saccades (Gao et al., 2018; Kunimatsu et al., 2018; Scerra et al., 2019; Tanaka, 2006; Wardak et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Neuroimaging studies suggest that network mechanisms in the parietal, frontal, and temporal lobes that control the programming of saccades overlap with those underlying covert attention.
source: Neuroimaging studies suggest that network mechanisms in the parietal, frontal, and temporal lobes that control the programming of saccades overlap with those underlying covert attention (Corbetta et al., 1998; Nobre et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: The premotor theory of attention proposes that the circuit used for generating movements is also active during attention shifts.
source: Along the same avenue, the 'premotor theory of attention' by Rizzolatti et al., 1987 proposes that the circuit used for generating movements is also active during attention shifts.
evidence: This is a citation to a theoretical framework from prior literature.

claim: It is not possible to attend to a covert cue when the cue is outside of the range of the oculomotor system.
source: This theory is also supported by the observation that the working peripheral location of the covert cue stimulus is restricted by the ultimate potential outer position of the eye in that it is not possible to attend to a covert cue when the cue is outside of the range of the oculomotor system (Craighero et al., 2004; Hanning and Deubel, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: At least part of the visual cells in the FEF that respond to covert attention do not modulate in relation to saccades.
source: For example, findings in the FEF show that at least part of the visual cells that respond to covert attention do not modulate in relation to the saccades, implying that there may be cell type – specificity for responses to covert attention in this region (Gregoriou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: Mo consistently outperformed Mi in task performance.
source: Mo consistently outperformed Mi, and this trend was present across different experimental sessions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral performance data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Mi's overall performance increase was mostly mediated by his improvement in the subset of up-/downward trials in the task.
source: The weight that Mi assigned to the U/D gap direction increased simultaneously with task performance. In contrast, the weight that was assigned to the L/R stimulus remained constant, suggesting that his overall performance increase was mostly mediated by his improvement in the subset of up-/downward trials in the task (Figure 1E, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by logistic regression modeling of behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mo exhibited increased weighting of the stimulus in both U/D and L/R trials.
source: Mo, on the other hand, exhibited increased weighting of the stimulus in both U/D and L/R trials.
evidence: This is supported by logistic regression modeling of behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mo's overall higher performance relative to Mi was reflected in the model by higher weights for the gap direction throughout all measured sessions.
source: Indeed, the overall higher performance of Mo relative to Mi was reflected in the model on Mo's data having higher weights for the gap direction throughout all measured sessions (Figure 1E, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by logistic regression modeling of behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mi assigned less weight to the previous saccade over time if the current trial was in the L/R direction.
source: According to this model, Mi assigned less weight to the previous saccade over time if the current trial was in the L/R direction (p = 0.016; R2 = 0.32, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by logistic regression modeling of behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no change in event weight to predict the response on the current trial in the past-trial variables for Mo.
source: In contrast, there was no change in event weight to predict the response on the current trial in the past-trial variables for Mo.
evidence: This is supported by logistic regression modeling of behavioral data.

claim: 305 DN neurons were recorded while the animals performed the Landolt C task.
source: Single-unit activity was recorded for 305 DN neurons, while the animals performed the Landolt C task.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: The activity levels of DN neurons in both Mi and Mo changed during the instruction and movement stage, depending on the stimulus identity.
source: The activity levels of DN neurons in both Mi and Mo changed during the instruction and movement stage, depending on the stimulus identity (Figure 2B, D; for separate datasets of Mi and Mo, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cells could show significant facilitation of their activity in a window associated with the C-stimulus or the saccade relative to baseline activity.
source: For example, cells could show significant facilitation of their activity in a window associated with the C-stimulus (200 ms moving window, 100 ms steps from 0 to 800 ms after C-stimulus onset) or the saccade (200 ms moving window, 100 ms steps from −200 ms before to 200 ms after saccade onset) relative to baseline activity from before trial onset (see Material and methods for details) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cells could show suppression of their firing following the C-stimulus and the saccade.
source: Likewise, cells could also show suppression of their firing following the C-stimulus and the saccade (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The population of suppressing neurons exhibited modulation significantly earlier than facilitating units after C-stimulus onset.
source: When we aligned the neurons to the time of their maximum change in activity after C-stimulus onset, the population of suppressing neurons (n = 85) exhibited the modulation significantly earlier (p < 0.0041; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test) than did the facilitating units (n = 90), (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: There was no significant difference in timing between facilitating and suppressing cells during the saccade window.
source: This was not the case (p = 0.23) for facilitating (n = 57) and suppressing (n = 38) cells during the saccade window (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Many cells encoded the gap direction, the saccade or both, while a smaller fraction was sensitive to the events in the previous trial.
source: We found that many cells encoded the gap direction, the saccade or both, while a smaller fraction was sensitive to the events in the previous trial (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: This is supported by GLM analysis shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Many units showed firing rate modulation in relation to both particular gap directions and saccades.
source: Many units showed firing rate modulation in relation to both particular gap directions and saccades (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: This is supported by GLM analysis shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: A neural response after the saccade in trials where the animal made a mistake was a common feature.
source: Likewise, a neural response after the saccade in trials where the animal made a mistake was a common feature (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of error trials shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fractions of recorded neurons that were sensitive to particular task parameters were similar in both animals.
source: Despite the level of heterogeneity among the two NHPs in terms of performance level and strategy, the fractions of recorded neurons that were sensitive to particular task parameters, including gap direction, saccade direction, or miscellaneous were similar in both animals, indicating that we sampled from comparable populations of DN neurons in the two NHPs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by GLM analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The latency from the onset of the C-stimulus to the moment of ramping in Mo was on average 115 ms shorter than that of Mi.
source: We analyzed the ramping of firing rates in relation to the moment of the C-stimulus presentation (Satopaa et al., 2011), and found that the latency from the onset of the C-stimulus to the moment of ramping in Mo was on average 115 ms shorter (F = 10.9, p = 0.001) than that of Mi (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ramping onset analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The condition that was most reliably represented in the decoding model was the trial outcome.
source: The condition that was most reliably represented was the trial outcome, that is, whether the monkey made a correct or incorrect choice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The proportion of cells from which the trial outcome could be decoded increased at about 1 s following the presentation of the C-stimulus and persisted throughout the delay period.
source: The proportion of cells from which the trial outcome could be decoded increased at about 1 s following the presentation of the C-stimulus to the monkey, and this persisted throughout the delay period and remained present for more than a second after the monkey had made his choice (Figure 4A, see different columns).
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Compared to Mo, Mi had more cells from which the trial outcome could be decoded around the time of the reward.
source: Compared to Mo, Mi had more cells from which the trial outcome could be decoded around the time of the reward.
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mo showed many cells in which the gap direction could be decoded, which is relevant to making a correct choice.
source: Instead, Mo showed many cells in which we could decode information about the C-stimulus, including the gap direction, which is relevant to making a correct choice.
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mi had more cells than Mo that maintained information about the choice he had made in the previous trial, well into the time-frame of the ongoing trial.
source: In line with the findings of the behavioral model, Mi instead had more cells than Mo that maintained information about the choice he had made in the previous trial, well into the time-frame of the ongoing trial.
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There were almost no cells from which the gap direction of the past trial could be decoded in either NHP.
source: Lastly, there were almost no cells from which the gap direction of the past trial could be decoded in either NHP (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The injections were focused on the centrolateral part of the DN positioned in the center of its rostrocaudal axis.
source: In both cases, the injections were focused on the centrolateral part of the DN positioned in the center of its rostrocaudal axis; given the distribution of the modulating cells according to the stereotactic coordinates with respect to the 2D-grid of the recording chamber and the recording depths, we estimated that the functionally relevant recording area covered a vertical column of approximately 2 mm long, 2 mm wide, and 3 mm deep, as all modulated cells were recorded in a square of that size.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The size of the injection was bigger in Mo as compared to Mi.
source: Despite a similar location for the core of the injection site, the size of the injection was bigger in Mo as compared to Mi, possibly reflecting different stock preparations or anisotropic spread of the tracer.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In Mi the dorsolateral and ventrolateral leaf of the principal olivary nucleus contained 38 and 78 cells, respectively, while the ventrolateral outgrowth of the PO contained only 4 cells.
source: In Mi the dorsolateral and ventrolateral leaf of the principal olivary nucleus (PO) contained 38 and 78 cells, respectively, while the ventrolateral outgrowth of the PO contained only 4 cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In Mo, 1977, 763 and 312 neurons were counted in the dorsolateral leaf, ventrolateral leaf, and ventrolateral outgrowth of the PO, respectively.
source: Instead, in Mo we counted 1977, 763 and 312 neurons in the dorsolateral leaf, ventrolateral leaf, and ventrolateral outgrowth of the PO, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The labeling in the PO of the IO was in line with the retrograde labeling in the pons, which was predominantly confined to the medial pontine nuclei in both Mi and Mo.
source: The labeling in the PO of the IO was in line with the retrograde labeling in the pons, which was predominantly confined to the medial pontine nuclei in both Mi and Mo, with Mo showing more labeled cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mo showed more retrogradely labeled Purkinje cells (n = 1314) than Mi (n = 84).
source: Likewise, Mo showed more retrogradely labeled Purkinje cells (PCs; n = 1314) than Mi (n = 84), when we screened 1 out of 24 sections of the cerebellar cortex (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: Most of the labeled PCs appeared to be located in the D1 and D2 zones of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Most of the labeled PCs appeared to be located in the D1 and D2 zones of the cerebellar cortex (Voogd et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 5E and 5F, with reference to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Anterograde CTb labeling was found in the parvocellular and magnocellular red nucleus, zona incerta and deep mesencephalic nucleus as well as various thalamic nuclei.
source: In addition, we found anterograde CTb labeling in the higher brainstem; this included for example the parvocellular and magnocellular red nucleus, zona incerta and deep mesencephalic nucleus as well as various thalamic nuclei, such as the ventrolateral thalamic nucleus (VL), pulvinar nucleus (Pul), mediodorsal thalamic nucleus (MD), and centromedial and centrolateral thalamic nuclei (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: No substantial labeling was found in the superior colliculus, ventral tegmental area or hypothalamus.
source: Instead, we did not find substantial labeling in the superior colliculus, ventral tegmental area or hypothalamus.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the anatomical tracing study.

claim: The labeled areas are consistent with previous studies illustrating disynaptic pathways from the DN to cerebral cortical areas involved in visual processing such as the FEF area.
source: The labeled areas we found are consistent with previous studies illustrating disynaptic pathways from the DN to cerebral cortical areas involved in visual processing such as the FEF area (Kipping et al., 2013; Middleton and Strick, 2001; Romanski et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with prior anatomical studies.

claim: DN cells connected with the D1 and D2 zones in the cerebellar cortex have highly diverse activity patterns.
source: Accordingly, we found that DN cells connected with the D1 and D2 zones in the cerebellar cortex have highly diverse activity patterns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological and anatomical data.

claim: DN neuron activity frequently shows both upbound and downbound modulations, similar to PCs in the lateral cerebellum that project to the DN.
source: Their activity often bridges different experimental epochs and frequently show both upbound and downbound modulations (De Zeeuw, 2021), similar to PCs in the lateral cerebellum that project to the DN (Avila et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiological data and comparison with prior studies.

claim: Following training of the task, many DN neurons respond in a visual direction- or movement direction-selective manner more than half a second before the saccade of choice is made.
source: Importantly, following training of the task, many DN neurons respond in a visual direction- or movement direction-selective manner more than half a second before the saccade of choice is made.
evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiological recordings and temporal analysis.

claim: The region where recordings were made in the DN forms part of the cerebellar D1 and D2 microcomplex.
source: The distribution of the retrogradely labeled PCs in lateral lobules VII and VIII as well as crus I/II indicates that the region where we recorded in the DN forms part of the cerebellar D1 and D2 microcomplex (De Zeeuw, 2021; De Zeeuw and Ten Brinke, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data and comparison with prior anatomical studies.

claim: The medial pons is known to receive direct input from the prefrontal cortex and to activate the D zones during decision making and motor planning.
source: This conclusion is supported by the retrograde CTb labeling we found in the part of the medial pons that is known to receive direct input from the prefrontal cortex and to activate the D zones during decision making and motor planning (Buckner et al., 2011; Prevosto et al., 2010; Ramnani, 2012; Salmi et al., 2010; Stoodley and Schmahmann, 2010; Strick et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Most of the retrograde labeling in the olive following the injections in the DN was present in the dlPO and vlPO, which are part of the D1 and D2 modules.
source: Likewise, most of the retrograde labeling in the olive following the injections in the DN was present in the dlPO and vlPO, which are also part of the D1 and D2 modules (Voogd et al., 2012; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data and comparison with prior anatomical studies.

claim: Most anterogradely labeled fibers were found in the pulvinar, mediodorsal thalamus and ventrolateral thalamus, which are known to connect to various parts of the prefrontal cortex.
source: Most anterogradely labeled fibers were found in the pulvinar, mediodorsal thalamus and ventrolateral thalamus, which are known to connect to various parts of the prefrontal cortex, such as FEF and Brodmann area 46 (Kipping et al., 2013; Middleton and Strick, 2001; Romanski et al., 1997), and/or the parietal eye field, an established hub in the dorsal attention network (Andersen et al., 1992; Hanks et al., 2015; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Svoboda and Li, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data and citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: The dorsal attention network has been shown to connect to lobules VII and VIII.
source: Interestingly, the dorsal attention network has been shown to connect to lobules VII and VIII (Brissenden et al., 2016; Buckner et al., 2011), precisely the location of the cerebellar cortex where retrograde labeling was detected following the DN injections.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies and comparison with the anatomical tracing data.

claim: The anatomical findings suggest that the DN region under study is at least partly integrated in a functional closed loop between cerebellum and cerebral cortex that appears to be involved in decision making, planning, and attention.
source: Taken together, the anatomical findings suggest that the DN region under study is at least partly integrated in a functional closed loop between cerebellum and cerebral cortex that appears to be involved in decision making, planning, and attention.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical tracing data and comparison with prior studies.

claim: Individual DN cells can encode both the direction of the visual cue and the associated direction of the subsequent saccade.
source: Our data reveal that individual DN cells can encode both the direction of the visual cue and the associated direction of the subsequent saccade, suggesting that different task-specific activations in the cerebellar cortex may be relayed downstream to the same target neurons in the cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiological recordings and encoding model.

claim: Different task-specific activations in the cerebellar cortex may be relayed downstream to the same target neurons in the cerebellar nuclei.
source: Our data reveal that individual DN cells can encode both the direction of the visual cue and the associated direction of the subsequent saccade, suggesting that different task-specific activations in the cerebellar cortex may be relayed downstream to the same target neurons in the cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that individual DN cells encode multiple task parameters.

claim: Lateral lobules VIIb/VIIIa upstream of the DN exhibit functional properties characteristic of the dorsal attention network in the cerebral cortex.
source: Our data are compatible with and expand upon fMRI studies, which have demonstrated that lateral lobules VIIb/VIIIa upstream of the DN exhibit functional properties characteristic of the dorsal attention network in the cerebral cortex (Brissenden et al., 2018; Brissenden et al., 2016; van Es et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: Lobules VII and VIII in the cerebellar hemispheres show task-specific activation that depends on representation of visuospatial location and/or load of working memory.
source: Indeed, this part of the cerebellar hemispheres shows task-specific activation in that their responses depend on representation of visuospatial location and/or load of working memory (Brissenden et al., 2018; Brissenden et al., 2016; van Es et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: Injecting accelerations of simple spike modulations of PCs in the cerebellar hemispheres into the complex of cerebellar nuclei may be instrumental in improving the performance of responses to covert attention.
source: The difference in onset of DN ramping between the monkeys highlights the possibility that injecting accelerations of simple spike modulations of PCs in the cerebellar hemispheres into the complex of cerebellar nuclei may be instrumental in improving the performance of responses to covert attention, akin to what has been shown for the impact of PCs of the vestibulocerebellum on responses in the vestibular nuclei and compensatory eye movements upon vestibular stimulation (De Zeeuw et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, drawing an analogy to prior studies.

claim: Expert and amateur baseball players show cerebellar activation upon visual presentation of a pitched ball with different reaction times.
source: Likewise, our data on the differences in choice performance between Mo and Mi are also supported by the different reaction times in expert and amateur baseball players, who show cerebellar activation upon visual presentation of a pitched ball (Owens et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Electrophysiological studies have revealed a role of the cerebellar nuclei, including the DN, in motor planning.
source: Moreover, our recordings are corroborated by electrophysiological studies that have revealed a role of the cerebellar nuclei, including that of the DN, in motor planning (Chabrol et al., 2019; Deverett et al., 2019; Deverett et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: The DN cells recorded may contribute to the preparation of directed saccades through their projections to the FEF via the thalamus.
source: The DN cells recorded in the current study may contribute to the preparation of directed saccades through their projections to the FEF via the thalamus (Lindeman et al., 2021; Middleton and Strick, 2001; Romanski et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical connectivity and functional data, supported by citations.

claim: FEF neurons encode multiple aspects of saccade planning and processing, including target identification in covert visual searches.
source: Similar to our DN neurons, the FEF neurons that are embedded in the dorsal attention network encode multiple aspects of saccade planning and processing, including target identification in covert visual searches (Brissenden et al., 2018; Brissenden et al., 2016; Buckner et al., 2011; van Es et al., 2019), as well as decision making among multiple choices (Ding and Gold, 2012; Gregoriou et al., 2012; Hanes and Schall, 1996; Monosov and Thompson, 2009; Schall and Hanes, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: FEF neurons can show ramping activity before upcoming eye movements.
source: Accordingly, FEF neurons can show the type of ramping activity before upcoming eye movements (Basu and Murthy, 2020; Raghavan and Joshua, 2017) that we present here for the DN neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies and comparison with the current data.

claim: Ramping activity is one of the main signatures of motor preparation.
source: Given that such ramping activity is one of the main signatures of motor preparation (Chabrol et al., 2019; Deverett et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2018; Hanks et al., 2015; Svoboda and Li, 2018), DN neurons may have a critical role in facilitating the preparation of visuomotor processing in general.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: DN neurons may have a critical role in facilitating the preparation of visuomotor processing in general.
source: Given that such ramping activity is one of the main signatures of motor preparation (Chabrol et al., 2019; Deverett et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2018; Hanks et al., 2015; Svoboda and Li, 2018), DN neurons may have a critical role in facilitating the preparation of visuomotor processing in general.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of ramping activity in DN neurons and its known role in motor preparation.

claim: The cerebellum receives inputs from many different external sensory as well as internal cognitive modalities, all of which can be integrated during the preparation and execution of complex tasks.
source: The cerebellum receives inputs from many different external sensory as well as internal cognitive modalities, all of which can be integrated during the preparation and execution of complex tasks (De Zeeuw, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior review.

claim: At the input stage of the cerebellar cortex, activation of different sensory modalities has been shown to enhance spiking output of granule cells.
source: At the input stage, that is, at the level of the granule cells in the granular layer, activation of different sensory modalities has been shown to enhance spiking output (Giovannucci et al., 2017; Ishikawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Many individual granule cells can receive inputs from both the cuneate nucleus relaying sensory proprioceptive signals and the pontine nuclei mediating presumptive motor command signals.
source: Moreover, given that many individual granule cells can receive inputs from both the cuneate nucleus relaying sensory proprioceptive signals and the pontine nuclei mediating presumptive motor command signals (Guo et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2013; Wagner et al., 2019), it is likely that sensory, motor and cognitive signals can also be integrated at the level of the cerebellar input layer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: It is likely that sensory, motor and cognitive signals can be integrated at the level of the cerebellar input layer.
source: Moreover, given that many individual granule cells can receive inputs from both the cuneate nucleus relaying sensory proprioceptive signals and the pontine nuclei mediating presumptive motor command signals (Guo et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2013; Wagner et al., 2019), it is likely that sensory, motor and cognitive signals can also be integrated at the level of the cerebellar input layer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known convergence of different input types onto granule cells.

claim: Integration of various forms of sensory, motor, and/or cognitive signals occurs at the level of the DN neurons downstream of PCs in the D1 and D2 zones.
source: Our results demonstrate that integration of various forms of sensory, motor, and/or cognitive signals also occurs at the level of the DN neurons downstream of PCs in the D1 and D2 zones.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data showing multimodal encoding in DN neurons.

claim: Single DN neurons can encode the direction of a visual stimulus, as well as the preparation and execution of a saccadic eye movement into a particular direction.
source: Indeed, single DN neurons can encode the direction of a visual stimulus, as well as the preparation and execution of a saccadic eye movement into a particular direction.
evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiological recordings and encoding model.

claim: The encoding of both stimulus and saccade directions is present in the biggest proportion of task-modulated neurons in both monkeys.
source: The encoding of both stimulus and saccade directions is present in the biggest proportion of task-modulated neurons in both monkeys.
evidence: This is supported by the GLM analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Electrophysiological data on DN encoding during the Landolt C task are in line with fMRI studies showing covert attention signals in the cerebellum.
source: Our electrophysiological data on DN encoding during the Landolt C task are in line with fMRI studies showing covert attention signals in the cerebellum (Brissenden et al., 2018; Brissenden et al., 2016; van Es et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with prior fMRI studies.

claim: Most of the neurons in the DN exhibit heterogeneous modulations during putative attention shifts and subsequent goal-directed saccadic eye movements.
